title: Port
description:
A termination point on a resource, in the RFC 8345 sense: the thing a Link attaches to. Ports are modelled separately from Links so that an uncabled port is still a fact -- 'this switch has sixteen OSFP cages and four are empty' is exactly what a bring-up needs to know, and a link-only model cannot say it.

`port_class` spans network, PCIe, power, coolant and console on purpose. A coolant inlet and an OSFP cage have nothing physically in common, but they play the identical role in the topology graph, and one termination-point entity means reachability, expected-versus-observed and cable tracing work the same way for both. This is the IT/OT convergence, expressed in the data model rather than in a dashboard.

resource_id.description: The resource this port is on.

name.description: Port name as the device reports it and as the label reads: `OSFP1`, `eth0`, `mlx5_0`, `INLET_A`. Unique within its resource.

port_class.description: What kind of connection terminates here. Closed list, because the class determines which validations apply and an unrecognized class would silently skip all of them.

media.description: Physical medium or connector. Needed because a cabling plan that matches port names but mismatches media is a plan that fails at install time.

index.description: Ordinal position, for ports whose name does not sort usefully. `OSFP10` sorts before `OSFP2` as a string, and a cabling report in that order is unusable.

speed_gbps.description: Configured or negotiated speed. On an `expected` record this is the design speed; on an `observed` record it is what the link actually came up at, and the difference is one of the most common real defects.

lanes.description: Lane count, for split or breakout ports.

breakout_of.description: The physical parent port, when this is one channel of a breakout. A 4x split OSFP is one physical cage and four logical ports, and both views have to exist: the cage is what gets cabled, the channels are what come up.

part_location.description: Where the cage or connector physically sits, for a port on a large chassis where the name alone does not locate it.

identifiers.description: Port-level identity. IB_GUID and MACAddress are the common cases, and they are what discovery output joins on.

admin_state.description: Intended state. Separate from operational state, which is telemetry: a port that is administratively down is correct, and a monitoring system that conflates the two pages someone at 3am for a deliberate configuration.
